result: Focused source review: two small corrections recommended; no materially overstated daily-life claim found in the checked passages. This is not blanket verification of every source or of map geometry.
pointerConvention: Zero-based section and item indices within the named draft.

findings.sectionTitle: A written greeting and a political ending
findings.issue: The cited Transcription PDF uses Roman transliteration, not Arabic letters. The phrase is accurately recognizable Arabic, but the claim that this Arabic-script string appears in that transcription overstates what the cited witness displays. The reduced manuscript PDF is accessible, but web screenshot calls returned only a citation string to this reviewer, so I could not independently inspect its original letters.
findings.action: Either have a reviewer inspect manuscript page 1 and cite that witness, or label the displayed Arabic as a normalized Arabic rendering of the editors' transliteration. Safest immediate replacement: show Bismi l-Lāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm and say it is the editors' Roman-letter transcription of the Arabic invocation. Keep the distinction between this Arabic frame and the Hausa poem.
findings.evidence: Transcription PDF page 1 line 1 reads Bismi l-Lāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm. The English translation page 1 supports the meaning. Manuscript witness: https://sites.bu.edu/nehajami/files/2022/08/Hunwick-95-3_150ppi.pdf .

findings.sectionTitle: Family memory and a little written Yoruba
findings.issue: Crowther locator says printed p.77; the Bu water example is on printed p.67. The quoted Yoruba and English translation match the accessible OCR.
findings.action: Change p.77 to p.67 in this item's _locator and source af-par-oyo-crowther.note. Check the next item's locator too, since its corn/yam examples continue the same entry across the page boundary.
findings.evidence: Internet Archive full text lines 6087-6104; printed page marker 67 follows the water and corn examples. No wording change needed to the public sample.

knownIntegrationConcern.status: Root reported changing first period upper bound to circa 1490 for validation. Not a new historical criticism.

checkedSources.scope: 1852 title page and OCR Bu entry, water translation and adjacent corn/yam examples. Printed page marker checked; scan typography/diacritics not independently inspected.

Full archive introduction and Arabic title heading; supports copying/digitization, Wakar Bagauda identification and exact unvocalized title. English gloss independently read as a literal translation, not claimed as a quoted archive translation.
PDF pages 1-3 textual extraction, Arabic opening in Roman transliteration and Hausa verses.
PDF pages 1-3: invocation, ritual washing/dry ablution, charity and women's food/education/marital obligations.
BU manuscript landing page and linked reduced PDF. Original PDF has two pages and no extractable text. Original-script image could not be independently viewed through returned web output.
GMU scholarly excerpts, particularly Zaharatu childbirth care, Aisha orphans/widows, jajis and Asma'u's teaching. Claims remain attributed and do not generalize to universal practice.
Person chronology: 1860s rise, 1891 scorched earth, 1892 eastward displacement, April 1893 Umarian dismantling.
TDV scholarly biography capture on 29 September 1898 and exile/death in 1900, plus early state formation. Only these limited claims were checked, not every biographical interpretation.
Lofkrantz scholarly chapter: 1804-1903 caliphate, European conquest, Kano 1903, Ségou 1890 and Masina 1893. Supports narrative endings.

Original short URL failed, but the same Tunisia National Library record 5652875 with full Arabic slug loaded in search. Title, author, Tunis state press and 1876 volume 1 confirmed. Arabic gloss is a reasonable literal translation, not supplied by catalog.
Full NCMM tentative-list Description: staged walls, gates, Kurmi lanes and goods, Rumfa dates, palace household/service divisions. Card correctly qualifies present palace layout.
Research article abstract, tables and discussion: Oyo contexts 1570-1835, Terminalia/Senegalia and cautious explanations of household fuel variability. Card preserves uncertainty appropriately.
Full Bournemouth hosted survey page: palace courtyards, reservoir, market, six-metre Kosso walls and uncertain scaffolding holes.
Full Met object text: later date, materials, handling patina and memorial caregiving. Card correctly avoids presenting this as an imperial excavation or universal family practice.
Chapter 7 sections A and B: preconquest Middle Niger economy, Somono commerce, gun carriage/cannonball specialists and Markoya women/children/enslaved dependants. Public passages supported.

retrievalLimits: af-par-oyo-law opened as a Persée viewer without substantive article text in this review; the circa-1836 claim was not independently reverified here.

af-par-hausa-maghili attribution, other library/treasury objects, Samori arms/captive/Sordi evidence, Sokoto agricultural sources and remaining sources were not independently reopened in this focused review.

No polygon chronology or identity equivalence was independently audited. The bundle explicitly discloses Samori post-1898 and Sokoto post-1903 map-date problems; those disclosures do not validate the geometry.
Samori writing sample remains explicitly unverified. Keeping that stated gap is preferable to inserting unrelated regional Arabic text.
